Science.title: NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
Science.summary: NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.

Science.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
Science.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

Science.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

Science.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
Science.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

Sports.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
Sports.summary: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic
Culture.summary: Glyndebourne, Lewes Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache. For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss. Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are having connection problems of their own. But she can escape up the chimney to a rooftop land populated by Spark Monsters – who will help her regain her lost spark, pun intended. Continue reading...
